segments.text: I'm Gary Wymer and thanks for watching
Fox 35 News Plus as we talk with the
candidates for Florida governor in 2026.
Today we're sitting down with Republican
Congressman Byron Donald's.
>> Congressman, on this Saturday we are
catching up with you here at the
Villages. You just finished up a
campaign event talking to a couple
hundred people out there. It looked like
uh they had the chance to ask you a lot
of questions. So, just talk to me about
the campaign trail and what you're
seeing from voters that you're uh
getting the chance to talk to all across
the state.
>> Well, the campaign trail has been great.
Um, it's actually been a lot of events
like this. Uh, we've been in 50 counties
in Florida already. We're going to get
to the other 17. We're going to do a
couple reruns. Second time here in the
Villages. Really excited. I think the
biggest thing is, you know, it's about
talking about the issues that matter to
the people of Florida. Uh we do a lot of
Q&A sessions with voters where they just
come in, they have their question heard.
Uh sometimes it gets opened up to the
floor and we just see what else people
want to talk about. You want to make
sure you're addressing a couple of key
concerns. Number one, uh Governor
DeSantis has done a great job. People
want to make sure the state's going to
continue in the direction that is going.
We are committed to that. Um I voted for
a lot of his agenda when I was in the
state house. Uh his first two years as
governor and you know in my time in
Congress still standing for conservative
principles up there although it's a lot
harder to get it accomplished in
Washington for obvious reasons. Uh but
then number two talking about taxes,
insurance, water quality,
transportation, uh the future of the
state's economy, education for our kids.
These are all still going to be the
issues that need to be addressed going
forward. and I'm definitely prepared to
meet that challenge and excited for the
opportunity to leave Florida into the
future.
>> And we'll get into a lot of those uh
issues that we know are important to
Florida voters, but I first want to ask
you um why
potentially leave Congress to run for
governor here in Florida? What what made
you want to to to take that step and
make that decision? Well, first, um, you
know, Florida's future really does
matter to America, and our state's going
to need a governor who, number one,
knows the apparatus here in in Florida,
but then also in Washington. That's
going to be very important. Number two,
um, a governor who has really good ties
with the presidential administration to
be able to advocate for Florida's
interests at a moment's notice. That's
going to be critical, especially around
times of storms and things like that.
Um, but then the third thing is my
career, my background was in finance,
uh, financial services, banking,
insurance. These are all going to be
important things that the state's going
to have to figure out, especially
insurance going into the future. And
last but not least, Florida needs a
conservative governor to follow in the
footsteps of Ronda Santis, who is a
conservative governor. Um, and I fit
that bill as well. So, when it came time
to starting to think about that, um, I
decided probably the next thing for me
was to throw my hat in the ring and and
run for governor. And it's been going
very well. I'm very excited about the
progress, but we still have a long way
to go. We want to make sure we're
earning the vote of the people of
Florida.
>> You mentioned President Trump. You do
have the endorsement of President Trump.
I'm curious how that came about. Did he
talk to you about it ahead of time or uh
how did that how did that kind of go
down? I mean, he he and I talked about
it off and on, but mostly it was focused
on first, you know, helping him to get
elected u back in 2024 and then in early
2025 about the work on his agenda in
Congress. And um you know, he asked me,
he's like, "Is this what you want to
do?" And I said, "Yeah, it's what I want
to do." And you know, he was like,
"Okay." And he made a decision. Um I was
actually in Naples when he made the
decision to endorse me. Um I was in an
event with uh another member of Congress
and and people in Southwest Florida. And
so I got the phone call from the
president and you know obviously you got
to pick up his call and so I'm in the
middle of event. I answered his call and
he told me about it. So I'm incredibly
honored to have President Trump's
endorsement um because he doesn't give
it lightly. Um he has a lot of criteria
for it. But the number one thing is that
he wants his now home state to continue
to thrive, continue to be vibrant, and
that's why I'm honored to have his
endorsement to be Florida's next
governor.
>> Let's uh let's talk affordability. Those
were the first few questions we heard
here. Those are often the questions that
we hear. We know that is a top issue on
voters minds. How did we get here um to
where you know some say affordability
crisis here in the state of Florida
right [snorts] now? How did we get here?
>> Well, first of all, you got to
acknowledge the reality not just in
Florida but around the United States. Uh
what we had was terrible economic policy
from Joe Biden and the Democrats which
created an inflation that ripped through
our econ our entire economy and no
industry was safe from it. We all
remember coming out of COVID prices just
started skyrocketing and that's because
the Biden administration was spending so
much money at a time where they created
a labor shortage and that's how we got
to where we are here in Florida because
people were trying to escape New York,
Connecticut, New Jersey, Illinois,
California. Housing prices went up
because people were just buying property
in our state. That's how we got here.
The question is what are we going to do
about it? I think number one obviously
what the governor wants to do around
property tax elimination for homesteaded
Floridaidians I fully support the
governor's plan hope he and the
legislature can get to an agreement so
we can get that on the ballot this year.
Uh when it comes to insurance like I
said out there the governor and the
legislature did some very important tort
reforms around around property insurance
and auto insurance that are beginning
that are stabilizing rates in property
and casualty and auto insurance rates.
Those rates are coming down. Uh we want
to continue to follow up on that work
and then re-examine the state's entire
insurance regulatory framework so we can
find ways to bring new carriers into the
state, continue to allow for more
competition which will further push
insurance rates down. But then those are
the first two. But number three overall
is how do you build out the homes that
we're going to need going forward? We
want to be efficient with people's time.
We don't want to have people bogged down
in red tape and bureaucracy when they're
trying to build new homes and build in
some respects new apartments because
when you have dead time in projects
that's not free. It still costs the
enduser that money. The developers and
the contractors, they don't pay that
bill. It's passed on to the consumer. So
from a government side, we want to be
efficient with the development of these
projects. If you can build housing more
quickly, it actually decreases the cost
of housing. that's going to have a major
impact for the future of our state.
>> I was going to ask about housing costs
and housing supply and how do you
balance that as well with making sure we
don't overdevelop as a state.
>> Listen, overdevelopment is something I
don't want. Nobody wants to see that. I
think we have to be strategic about
planning the future of the state's
growth uh by regions. I think that's
going to be very important. It's about
getting the various counties in the
region on the same page about permitting
timelines about where you're going to
build housing and where you're going to
maintain the rural fringe, where you're
going to protect agriculture lands,
where you're going to protect
conservation areas, where you're going
to protect water quality. That's all
important. It's a part of the beauty of
Florida. And you know, as I've traveled
the state, I like I said, I've been in
50 counties. Um, in my time in
government, whether that's in Congress
the last five years or in the state
house the four years before that, I've
been in every county in our state. We
have a beautiful state that we want to
maintain. We want to protect. But you
also have a have to have a plan for how
you're going to build the new housing
that we're going to need into the
future. If you don't do that, then
what's going to happen is the price of
all housing is going to continue to go
up. And that's not in the best interest
of Flityians either.
Look, I I do want to ask you about
property taxes and the concerns we heard
from from one uh voter out here today
about about what it means for for
revenue of local governments and some of
the services that uh that we rely on and
uh you know that is something that we
have seen in polling is a is a concern
of of folks all around uh Florida about
what the impact would be. I think
everyone would like to say, "Well, I
don't want to, you know, I don't have to
pay property taxes." That's great. But
how do you address some of those
concerns about what it would mean for uh
the services that local communities and
and people rely on?
>> Well, look, I support what the governor
is trying to accomplish. Um I want to
make sure that our our uh sheriffs, our
police officers, firefighters, uh the
road construction, our schools, uh our
maintenance, that stuff, it continues to
be handled. Um looking forward to seeing
the governor's plan. his plan is going
to be detailed to address all these
things. And I think he working with the
legislature, that's where a lot of the
details around this very question you're
talking about are really going to get uh
hammered out. Um if they're not able to
accomplish something, then it's going to
be my responsibility as state's next
governor to pride to try to provide that
relief for homeowners in our state
because that is important. We have to
remember that people who make Florida
their home, they're not a piggy bank for
local governments. And so local
governments do have a responsibility to
contain their costs, control their
costs, lower them where they can because
seniors on fixed incomes or young
families just starting out, they don't
have the resources to just pay higher
and higher property taxes. So there's a
real balance there. I I think removing
homestead property taxes is important
for the future of the state, but we have
to balance that and mitigate that with
what we have to do to continue services.
But like I said out there, around 75 to
80% of all property taxes in our state
are non are nonhomestead property taxes.
About 20 to 25% are homestead property
taxes. So there's a way where we can
still address the needs uh that local
governments have that citizens have for
services which are critical. uh garbage
pickup, wastewater treatment facilities,
all those issues that local government
has to manage while also not increasing
the cost burden on people who call
Florida their home.
>> Let's talk about immigration. We know
right now the state is playing a a large
role when it comes to uh illegal
immigration enforcement um and getting
national attention for uh you know the
the kind of role that that we're playing
as a state right now. Would that um
continue uh under a Donald's
administration? Yes, it's going to
continue. We are going to continue to
cooperate with President Trump and his
team around supporting the frankly the
mandate from the American people. Um I
was on the campaign trail with the
president just as much as anybody. Um
it's a mandate from the American people
no matter what part of the state of the
country we were in. It was clear
Americans wanted to see criminal illegal
aliens being sent back to their home
countries and they wanted to see the
border secured. The border secured is a
mission accomplished from President
Trump. He's already been able to do
that. Now, it's the responsibility of
states working with the federal
government to get these criminal illegal
aliens out of our state and out of our
country. And we're going to be committed
to that work the same way Governor
DeSantis is.
>> There have been some questions and
concerns about due process for um these
people who've been detained. How do you
respond to those questions and concerns?
>> Well, first of all, if you're in the
country illegally, you do not have the
same level of due process as an American
citizen. Let's be very clear on this.
The Constitution is clear. The Supreme
Court has been clear on this. There is
not the same level that you or I or any
citizen of our country would have with
respect to due process. You simply do
not because you're not in the country
legally. And so there is a process to go
through deportation. There is an there
is what happens now is your identity is
checked, your documentation is checked.
If you're here illegally in the country,
then we go through that p that process
before the the deportation detainer is
issued and then you're removed from the
United States. That is the due process
afforded to an illegal alien in the
United States. But it needs to be
understood by frankly everybody. This is
not even a political question. For all
people in our country, all citizens in
our country, the level of due process
for an American citizen is not the level
for an illegal alien. Just like if an
American citizen goes abroad, you do not
maintain American uh uh uh due process
at the standard of the United States
Constitution and of American law. If
you're in another country, you simply
don't.
>> After the ICE shooting in Minnesota this
week, we heard the Democratic mayor of
Minneapolis say that having ICE agents
and a and a presence like that in
communities causes chaos. What do you
say about that?
>> He's a clown. The mayor of Minneapolis
is a fool. He's And part of the reason
that Minneapolis is in the shape that
it's in is because of him. The reality
is is that you cannot have sanctuary
jurisdictions in your country. How do
you have a situation where there are
rules in a city that are different from
the federal rules when it comes to
immigration? That dislocation is not
being brought by the federal government
or the Trump administration. that's
being brought by people like uh Mayor
Fry, like people like Governor Walls, uh
Governor Nuome, uh Governor Pritsker,
Governor Hokll, uh probably probably
we'll find out very shortly. He's
already talked about it. Uh Mayor
Mandani in New York, they are the ones
creating these dislocations and these
issues, not federal law enforcement. We
have to understand that when Joe Biden
was president of the United States, they
were not following federal immigration
law. They were ignoring that law. They
were subverting the law. They were not
enforcing it. Donald Trump won a
political mandate. He swept the
battleground states. He won the popular
vote on the mandate of securing this
nation and deporting criminal illegal
aliens. So, if you're a mayor in
Minneapolis, you don't have the legal
authority to stop ICE from actually
following federal law. You don't have
that ability. You can make whatever
statement you want, but it doesn't
coincide. It doesn't coincide with the
law. And I will add, especially in light
of the shooting, it's people like Mayor
Fry that have incited a lot of this
unrest where people don't know which
which way is coming or going because
they're gaslighting. They're issuing
propaganda. He's told ICE that they have
to get out of Minneapolis for it in
order for it to be safe. That is a lie.
Simply not true. The truth is you have
some of these Democrat officials who are
either directly in cahoots or fully in
support of these front groups, these
paid for front groups, these paid
agitators who were trying to stop ICE
from continuing its mission. And that's
simply not going to be tolerated in the
state of Florida. I can't worry about
the state of Minnesota. But what's
happening there is wrong. And a lot of
the images people are seeing on TV now
is because you have Democrat officials
who want wide open borders. They want no
immigration checks. They want our
communities to be overrun. And that is
not fair and it's not right to the
American people. People trying to find a
way just to make ends meet and build the
American dream for themselves.
>> Let's talk education. I know uh it's an
issue that is important to you and to
your wife as well. Yes. Um I we've we've
talked a lot about school vouchers in
Florida and you're seeing u you know
parents obviously have a lot uh we're
seeing the appetite uh for that. How do
you make sure though that uh the public
schools are still adequately funded as
they lose students?
>> Well listen first of all uh funding in
the public school system is predicated
on enrollment. If people if children are
enrolled in traditional public schools,
the money follows the child. The same
way if a parent decides they want to
enroll their child in a private school
or a charter school or they want to
homeschool, the money follows a child
that way as well. So if for the
superintendent of our in our state in a
traditional public schools in our state,
if you want to have more students
enrolling in your schools, you got to
make sure you're providing a better
output. That's what we should be doing.
Listen, I think that we should be
funding the education of the public.
That's been my position for more than 15
years. And what that means is the money
follows the child. If traditional public
schools want more enrollments in their
schools, then you have to do a better
job. And you have to prove to parents
that you're doing a better job. That's
what matters. Um, in terms of that's how
they get their funding today. And let's
talk about on the local level, property
taxes. Every school district in our
state is a taxing district. They have
the ability to leverage pop property
taxes, and they all do. And what's
happening in a lot of our large counties
is that their populations are
decreasing, but they're still leveraging
the property taxes. So, how is that fair
to the taxpayer? We're always going to
have a traditional public school system
in our state primarily because the
public schools have more infrastructure
than anybody. They have more seats than
anybody. They have more buildings than
anybody. They have the football fields.
They have the basketball gyms. They got
the baseball fields. And they got the
weight rooms. So, they're always going
to be a part of Florida. But the decider
of where that money goes is going to be
parents. Parents are at the head of the
table in the state of Florida. That will
remain.
>> Do you think teachers are paid enough
here?
>> Um I think teachers um we got to find
ways to pay them more. I think so. And
we got to be creative about ways that we
do it. Um but let's be clear, teachers
are professionals. They need to be
treated like professionals. Right now,
as we pay teachers, we don't treat them
as professionals.
It's a sliding scale payment system in
Florida. and you're ba you're paid the
same base rate and then you get
additional kickers based upon how many
years that you serve or or how many
other credentials that you have. That's
how we pay our teachers in Florida. I
would love teachers to be paid as
professionals. You are paid for how well
you do. And I think that's what
everybody would want to see. That's my
opinion.
>> Higher education, it's been years since
uh Florida has had to raise uh institute
in instate tuition.
uh is that something that you would like
to see continue and would it be feasible
to see continue into the future?
>> I don't think it's feasible to have to
raise uh tuition in our state because
look at the output of our university
system. We have the best university
system in the country. Our young people
are graduating with great degrees. Um
the thing I want to see going forward is
that we make sure that they're
graduating with degrees that are
economically viable. Every college
degree is not the same. Let's be honest
about that. And if you're going to talk
about college education at large, let's
also talk about making sure that our
kids coming out of high school are on a
pathway to success. It's not just about
going to the university system. It's
about what credential do you need?
What's going to help you put food on the
table? What's going to help you be able
to raise a family? What's going to be
able to help you pay your rent and
actually or pay your mortgage if if
you're abil have an ability to buy a
home? And whether it's high school, the
state college system, or the state
university system, we want every child
in Florida to be on a pathway to
economic success. That's going to be the
future of Florida. In terms of tuition
in the university system, um I see no
reason why we would even need to talk
about raising tuition because last time
I checked, when I see some of our
universities, the buildings all look
great and new. The kids are getting
degrees and they're working hard every
single day in our classrooms. So, it's
not about raising tuition. That's not
the answer. It's about making sure our
kids are on a pathway to viability. And
as long as our kids are on a pathway to
being economically viable, having the
skills they need, having the credentials
they need, and the training they need,
then I don't think we have to worry
about raising revenues.
>> Healthcare. Um, if the Obamacare uh
subsidies expire, we've seen reports of
premiums going through the roof in some
cases. There's no state that could be
impacted more by that than Florida
because of the number of folks uh who
who use those, you know, similar plans.
>> Do you believe the state should play a
role in uh doing more to to kind of help
with that
>> with subsidies
>> with uh affordable health care for uh
for folks when it comes to um you know
things like Medicaid and things like
that? Should there be a larger role that
the state plays to to make sure costs
stay down for people?
>> Well, first and foremost, we're not
going to expand Medicaid in our state.
Medicaid expansion in other states has
really put a major burden on those
states where their budgets have
ballooned and they really have no way of
getting costs under control, which then
bleeds into the taxpayer and then the
taxpayer has to come up with more money.
We were talking about affordability
earlier. The only one of the things that
will make our state less affordable is
Medicaid expansion because the ugly
truth is the federal government cannot
continue to pay for Medicaid expansion
the way it was promised under Barack
Obama. Two, the Affordable Care Act or
really the unaffordable care act is not
helping. That entire program needs to be
reformed. So, it's not about Florida
doing more. It's about the federal
government doing what is right, which is
reforming that that health insurance law
so people have more options to get
lowerc cost policies that they can
afford while still accessing health
care. That's going to be critically
important going forward. Subsidies going
to health insurance companies is not the
answer. And the only people advocating
for that are the Democrats and insurance
companies. They're advocating for it.
And I get the cost burden on people
because they went to go reapply for
their health insurance or seeing these
premiums spike. But let's be clear about
why that is. It's because Obamacare is
broken. It was written and designed for
health insurance premiums to
consistently rise over time. And the
answer from the Democrats would be, oh
well, we just need singlepayer health
care or we just need Medicaid for all.
That's actually the Bernie Sanders plan.
That's the AOC plan. That's what they
want to do. that is not going to be the
answer for health insurance and health
care costs in Florida or anywhere else
in America. So my position is clear. Uh,
Senator Rick Scott, our senator,
Representative August Fluger of Texas,
they have a very good bill that would
reform the Affordable Care Act space,
actually decrease health insurance
premiums for people here in Florida and
all through the country where you
wouldn't have to go and borrow money
from America's future, from America's
kids to pay for health insurance
premiums today. That's the actual
answer. And let's be very clear, these
subsidies, they don't fix the problem.
They just cover the problem. We have to
actually have real solutions that have
real results in the lives of people.
That's what should we should be doing
going forward.
>> Vaccine mandates. Yes, there's a lot of
talk about eliminating those, but
there's also we see concern from parents
who send their kids to school and and
don't want to see, you know, some of
those things spread. Where do you stand
on that? and how do you address uh some
of those uh concerns?
>> Well, look, I've already answered this
in a couple of areas. When it comes to
the vaccines that came out through uh
rulemaking, uh I think that those should
not be mandated. That stuff was not
mandated by the state legislature,
signed by any governor in the history of
our state. That stuff that the
Department of Health just threw on the
mandated list. I have three sons, okay?
I've seen the vaccination schedule
change from my oldest son who was 22 to
the one who's 14. and it's been more
vaccines required from the 14-y old and
from a 22 year old. That hasn't changed
the health criteria of my sons. So,
that's number one. Number two, when it
comes to the ones that are mandated, I
think there's a serious conversation
that's going to be had about polio, the
polio vaccine. That's something that
only the state legislature uh can pass
through both chambers. We'll see what
the legislature gets accomplished this
year. What I do want to see, I want
parents to be able to make far more
decisions about these vaccines. Even in
Florida law today, a parent can choose a
religious exemption to not vaccinate
their children if that's what they want
to do. That's in Florida law now. We'll
see where the governor ends up with. I
know they have a desire to go directly
to informed consent. I've talked to the
surgeon general about this, Mr. Latapo,
about his desire to go to fully to
informed consent. I think there's merit
to that, but there has to be a real
dialogue around polio, smallox. I think
those two vaccines that have been around
for a very long time, but the others,
no, they should not be mandated. I think
those are ones where informed consent
should be enough. And I think you'll see
I think you'll see overall um let's take
um hepatitis B for a moment. Why are we
giving us a a four-month old hepatitis
B? Why are we giving them a hepatitis B
vaccine at four months old, two months
old, or wherever it is in the vaccine
schedule today? These are the real
conversations we need to have. I think
another solution is actually spreading
out the vaccine schedule. Why are we
having newborns being jabbed with all
these vaccines so early in life? If
anything, spread them out. Um, make sure
that the ones that were done in
rulemaking, which I think the governor
is already going to do, and I fully
support that, that those actually um are
informed consent vaccines, if a parent
chooses they want to do that, they can.
Um, and that's where we should be going
going forward.
>> We're almost out of time here. Want to
get to know you a little bit. Favorite
song on your campaign playlist.
Uh right now it's uh John Cena. My time
is now.
>> That's what plays when we go in and out.
So it's it's a good one.
>> And uh what would you say is your uh
your go-to meal when you've got maybe a
big event coming up or or something like
that? What what would you say is your
go-to?
>> I'm not really a foodie. So I'm just not
I'm not a foodie guy. I don't have like
a favorite meal. Um it's
what's close, what's good. Let's do
that. And you keep going. What's next
for you on the campaign trail?
>> Uh heading to Tampa and then I'm going
to be back in DC this week and then uh
next weekend I I don't even know where I
am next. I got to look back at the
calendar. We're everywhere. Uh you know,
we're using every day possible to
campaign and get around the state. And
um you know, I'm excited about that. Um
might try to see if we get to get to
Miami for the national championship. See
if we can get in there for that.
>> All right. Be rooting for the Canes in
that one. That'll be something
different.
>> I'm I'm a seminal. It's different. And I
haven't I haven't done this one before,
but that's all right. No, I hope they
win. Uh they've done a great job this
year. They have a great team and uh
yeah, I watched I watched the game last
night in Indiana looks tough.
>> Yeah, they're going to be tough to beat.
Congressman Donald's, we appreciate it.
>> Awesome. Thank you.
